picks.style: ancient greek tragic chorus, aulos, bowed lyre, frame drum, layered female voices, slow and building, ominous
picks.why: A pure choral ode on the monsters of earth and sea and the worse thing that is human passion — one unbroken voice.

picks.style: ancient chorus, hand drums, low strings, massed voices with a lead, driving, inexorable, hammer-like pulse
picks.why: 'The anvil of Justice is planted firm' — Destiny forging a sword; a hard, concrete image with a beat already in it.

picks.style: greek funeral chorus, sparse lyre, deep drone, women's voices in unison, very slow, desolate
picks.why: 'What atonement is there for blood fallen to earth?' — the lament that sets the whole play going, and it stands alone.

picks.style: roman comic prologue, tibia double pipe, plucked lyre, brash patter tenor, brisk, sly, direct to the audience
picks.why: 'I bring you Plautus, with my tongue, not with my hand' — a single voice working a crowd, complete in itself.

picks.style: frenzied comic aria, aulos, clattering percussion, wild tenor, fast and accelerating, mock-tragic
picks.why: The feigned madness — axe, chariot, whip, 'Speed onward, ye steeds' — pure theatrical delirium built to be sung.

picks.style: grumbling patter song, tibia, hand drum, exasperated baritone, moderate, wry
picks.why: One unbroken rant at a wife who interrogates every exit: 'I've surely brought home a custom-house officer as my wife'.

picks.style: aquatic art song, harp, celesta, glass harmonica, floating soprano, undulating, weightless
picks.why: 'Down, down a thousand fathom deep' — a whole sea-nymph's song, self-contained and made of motion.

picks.style: moonlit gothic pastoral, harp, flute, light soprano with soft chorus, gentle, questioning, silvered
picks.why: Fairy footprints on morning sand and the call for the sprites to return — a complete small enchantment.

picks.style: romantic parlour song, fortepiano, viola, expressive mezzo, pensive, unhurried
picks.why: An address to the illusions of the imagination that opens and closes cleanly; the whole gothic sensibility in one lyric.

picks.style: restoration drinking catch, harpsichord, viol, recorder, hearty male chorus, moderate, convivial
picks.why: A bloodless feast where only the grape bleeds, love banished from the table — a toast that already scans as a round.

picks.style: baroque lament, chamber organ, viola da gamba, grave countertenor, slow, funereal, cavernous
picks.why: Death's vault with skulls for paving and rows of hourglasses labelled in blood — a startling, entirely visual passage.

picks.style: restoration memento mori ode, theorbo, consort of viols, declamatory baritone, stately, sardonic
picks.why: 'This grim Serjeant takes no Bail', then the schemer's mossy skull in the heap — grim wit with a clean turn.

picks.style: english tavern song, fiddle, squeezebox, rowdy male chorus, brisk, comic, foot-stamping
picks.why: The drunk coachman's retort — 'soakers like me enable you brewers to ride in your coaches' — a joke that lands on the last line.

picks.style: scots-inflected comic ballad, fiddle, bodhran, gruff male voice with a laughing chorus, lively, deadpan
picks.why: 'We shall go, one and all, where we find the best beer', then the man carried headless to the surgeon — two clean punchlines.

picks.style: sailor's shanty, concertina, stamping feet, gang vocal, swinging, irreverent
picks.why: The sailors confess, decide the priest is now carrying the weight, and throw him overboard — perfect shanty logic.

picks.style: italian sacred polyphony, organ drone, low bells, tenor cantus with choral answer, very slow, luminous, cathedral reverb
picks.why: Dante's order of the universe — all natures borne to different havens across the vast sea of being — in Italian and English together.

picks.style: sardonic german cabaret, harmonium, cello, biting baritone, march tempo, mock-solemn with swelling brass
picks.why: 'Is this the German way?' returns as a refrain over censers and Ave-bells — a polemic already shaped as a song.

picks.style: roman declamation with cithara, sparse lyre, solemn male voice, measured, ceremonial, spacious
picks.why: A father's cry of joy that son and grandson compete in virtue, ending 'far better is he than his father' — short and whole.
